Function report · 2026

Design at Ligentia: how the function works, what it delivers, and what it needs

How design currently operates, what the function has delivered, where its time goes, the tooling position, and where design could contribute more.

Prepared for
Boris, CIO
Prepared by
Craig, Design Lead
Date
September 2026
Status
Version 01
00

Purpose

This site seeks to provide an insight into the Ligentia Design teams operations.

It covers how design currently operates, what the function has delivered, where its time goes, the tooling position, and where design could contribute more with your support.

In short

  • Design's primary concern is how the platform works for the people using it, not only how it presents. Usability testing on Shipment Approval measured tasks completing between 46% and 56% faster on L5 than L4.
  • The function is deliberately managed: a single cross-module work view, weekly stakeholder priority meetings, cross-functional design crits, and seventeen team goals reviewed monthly against a score.
  • A UX maturity benchmark now underway shows strong scores on process, delivery fidelity and communication, with research and customer evidence as the clear gap. CX have since supported including design in their plan to put BAs closer to customers, which would address it directly.
  • Design led the cross-team process review that fixed the collaboration friction AI-driven working changes had introduced across product, BAs, design and engineering.
  • No headcount request. The three things that would make the most difference are context on Ligentix One, a route to our customers, and clarity on the future of existing platform investments.
  • A full record of H1 delivery is available separately and linked in section 2.

01

What design does at Ligentia

Design's remit is the experience of the platform, not just its appearance. That covers five things:

  1. Understanding the user's working environment: what they are actually trying to get done, and under what pressure. In practice Environmental analytics that confirmed an overwhelmingly desktop, Windows and Chrome user base, and a wide spread of screen resolutions with a strong bias toward 1920x1080, both of which constrain what we design for.
  2. Understanding their goals and pain points: evidenced where possible, and explicit about where we are inferring. In practice Usability testing on the Milestones module with findings distributed to stakeholders; the UX maturity benchmark in section 2; composite persona research currently underway.
  3. Onboarding and education: getting users to competence, not just to the screen. In practice Userflow implemented into Delivery, Wayfinder and Shipment Approval; Guidde, which design advocated for and other teams have since adopted for their own customer communication.
  4. The experience of using the tools themselves, including consistency and reusability at platform scale. In practice Swift, the design system, which the maturity survey credits with a unanimous top score on whether the finished product reflects what design specified.
  5. A follow-up strategy to measure real usage and improve continuously. In practice Userflow event tracking, task-completion metrics from prototype testing, and SUS benchmarking, which design has run before and is scheduled to repeat this year.

Visual design is one part of point four, and the most visible part, which is why design is often understood as UI.

Some of this is fully operating today. Some is partly built and constrained. Section 2 sets out where each part actually stands, and what is needed to close the gaps.

02

What design delivers, and the case for it

An overview of what the team delivered in the first half of the year is in the H1 achievements report, covering tooling, research practice, module delivery and process. Rather than repeat it, this section sets out the case for why that work matters.

Design's impact: L4 versus L5

The clearest evidence of design's impact is the difference between L4 and L5: same company, same users, same domain, one built without a design function and one with.

L4 delivered what was asked of it. The functionality was there and the business ran on it. What was missing was a discipline responsible for the whole. When something was requested, internally or externally, it was built and placed in the platform, without a consistent view of where it belonged or how it related to everything already there. The result was a system that worked but was hard to use, hard to learn, and hard to build on, accumulating usability inconsistencies, with limited reusability at platform scale.

L5 receives consistent positive feedback on usability. Some features present in L4 are still missing, a matter of product roadmap sequencing rather than design scope, but the usability of the system as a whole is reported on positively and consistently.

L5 may look simple. That is the point. Reduced visual noise, consistency and reusability at scale are deliberate. The difficulty is that when something is simple and easy to use it goes unnoticed, and what goes unnoticed is the thinking required to make it that way.

Simple does not mean static. We have a goal currently in motion to evolve the visual styling, while holding onto the core principles of simplicity and usability that make the platform work.

This argument is not only qualitative. The usability study below measured L4 against L5 directly on Shipment Approval, and found task completion between 46% and 56% faster on the redesigned interface.

Where this bears on your stated pain point

The gap L4 exposed was not a delivery problem. It was the absence of anyone accountable for the experience of the platform as a whole, and for whether it stayed coherent as it grew. That is a specific and containable risk in any ground-up rebuild, and it is the one design exists to hold. L5 is the evidence of what changes when it is held.

Advocacy in practice: the Settings module

A recent example of what that involves. Settings functionality was on course to be built independently within each module, which would have produced a fragmented configuration experience and repeated the L4 pattern in a new place.

Design argued for a centralised Settings module instead, including its potential to integrate with onboarding and materially reduce the time the onboarding process currently takes. Making that case required more than describing it: we built interactive prototypes so stakeholders could see what it would be, and sustained the advocacy until it was accepted. Settings is now adopted as a module and in active development.

This is the pattern I would want design applied to more often, and it is the argument for early involvement rather than review at the end.

UX maturity benchmark

I have been running a UX maturity survey, benchmarked against the Nielsen Norman Group six-stage scale, conducted as facilitated 1:1 sessions. Five interviews are complete, from July and August.

Caveat

The caveat comes first, because it determines how much weight the figures carry. All first five respondents have been Business Analysts. There are no engineering, QA, CX or leadership responses yet. What this currently measures is the BA–design relationship: the part of the process that breaks a problem down, collaborates on a solution, and delivers it to engineering. It is not a measure of Ligentia's organisational UX maturity.

On that basis:

Research and insight
3.6/5
Design process and collaboration
4.5/5
Output and communication
4.5/5
Influence and strategy
4.2/5

Two findings are worth your attention.

1. The foundations are in place.

The strongest scores are in how design works and what it delivers: process clarity (unanimous 5.0), build fidelity to specification (unanimous 5.0), communication of reasoning (4.8), ease of collaboration (4.6). Notably, the two perfect scores are attributed by respondents to interventions the design team introduced during this period: the cross-team process and the design system. Where we have changed how we work, the results are measurable.

2. The opportunity is in customer evidence.

The remaining gap is research and insight. The detail is encouraging: when design brings user evidence, it changes what gets built (4.2). What is missing is the evidence itself (2.6), and that reflects an organisational constraint rather than design capability. Research has consistently been design-initiated: Adrian's delivery sessions, prototype testing, concept validation. Respondents identify the barriers as time to conduct it, a route to customers, and a loop where business input is not reflected back before delivery.

Next step

Further interviews are scheduled. Completing the sample gives a baseline that can be tracked year on year, and I would want to bring the completed version into the goals review.

SwiftDS: capacity and its next stage

Design and engineering have both been design system advocates from the start. Together we made the case for SwiftDS and built it, and it now underpins our current products. The maturity survey attributes a unanimous top score on build fidelity to it, so its value is demonstrable.

However, design system technology is moving. They are increasingly built to support AI agents, and making progress in that direction was one of our goals at the start of the year. Agent infrastructure around a design system can catch component drift, enforce consistency rules, keep documentation in sync and support engineers directly, which frees both designers and engineers for higher-value work.

This is dependent on engineering capacity to implement, and that capacity has been the limiting factor throughout the year. SwiftDS has never been treated as a product in its own right, so prioritisation has been set on an ad hoc basis behind other internal needs, with progress pushed by design and engineering when capacity allowed.

Next step

Agree how SwiftDS should be classified and prioritised, and the dedicated resource its next stage would require.

The SwiftDS restyle: not looking auto-generated

One principle underneath the SwiftDS restyle is worth stating plainly: our design explorations should not look auto-generated.

There is a lot of enthusiasm at the moment for what AI agents can produce in the interface, and it is happening in many places at once. The output is fast and competent, but it converges: the models draw on the same conventions, so much of it arrives looking the same.

My expectation is that this corrects. As more products are built this way, businesses will want their own character and identity restated in what they put in front of customers. So the restyle is aiming at patterns with more personality than the layouts an agent reaches for by default, while holding onto the simplicity and usability that make the platform work.

A route to customers through CX

I have been talking to counterparts across teams to understand how ways of working are changing following the move, and to establish where design now fits.

The most useful thing to come out of that is on the CX side: CX have a plan to put BAs closer to customers. I have asked Julia whether design can be included in that space, and Richard Gane has supported it and is setting up a meeting to discuss.

If it happens, it addresses the weakest dimension in the benchmark above directly: a route to gathering insight from customers, and to observing them using the software, which matters more because what people do differs from what they report. Moving from reacting to reported issues toward a more evidence-led way of working has significant potential.

I am pursuing this already, so it is not an ask, but your support would carry more weight than mine alone.

Next step

Follow up with Richard on arranging the meeting.

Team goals: design's forward view

There have not been clearly defined business, product or design goals for the team to align to. Rather than work without direction, I set the design team's own: a structure of seventeen goals, agreed with Anthony Plummer, my senior stakeholder at the time, reviewed fortnightly and scored monthly.

Why goals and not a roadmap

A roadmap implies committed dates and fixed sequencing. Goals are deliberately more flexible: they let us shift emphasis between them as product priorities move, pausing some and pushing others without the whole plan becoming out of date. Given how often priorities change, that flexibility is a feature rather than a compromise, and it means design keeps a stated direction to work toward while staying responsive to what the product team needs.

The purpose is to ensure the team is not simply delivering against incoming requests, but actively developing its capability and moving the platform experience forward. They cover new ways of working and tooling, user-focused improvements to the platform, design system development, communication and visibility, and building a better understanding of how people actually use our products.

Not all are active in any given month; they are prioritised against live delivery work, and some are deliberately paused when capacity is required elsewhere. They are set as stretch goals, so scores are expected to sit below maximum. A run of 3s is the intended state, not underperformance.

Two things about how it has been run that are worth more than the scores:

  • Goals get closed when they stop earning their place. Roadmap visibility, a goal to get teams aligned on roadmaps, was retired in April after three months without traction, and the effort redirected.
  • External blocks are recorded as such. Swift improvements have been constrained by engineering capacity rather than design effort, and are scored accordingly rather than written up as progress.

Views: putting users in control of what they see

Views is a phased programme of work, defined by a collaborative design and front-end engineering workshop, giving users control over how data is presented to them within the platform. This type of functionality is frequently fed back as one of the biggest friction points for users. However getting this prioritised remains challenging.

The first release would introduce column visibility, ordering, and aliases, allowing users to surface the data most relevant to their role and hide what is not. Subsequent releases are planned to introduce more granular, in-context configuration options, with the intention of rolling the full Views capability across all modules via the design system.

Next step

Review the goals together. They were set for the year against a different organisational shape, so it is worth agreeing whether they are still appropriate.

Usability testing: the L4/L5 comparison, measured

In July 2025 the team ran a usability study directly comparing the existing L4 Shipment Approval interface against the redesigned L5 version, to establish whether the design changes actually improved task efficiency rather than just looking better.

Seventeen participants took part, none from Ligentia. The table content was replaced with generic data unrelated to supply chains, so nobody could rely on domain knowledge and the test measured the interface itself rather than familiarity with the business. That is a deliberately conservative setup: it tests learnability for someone encountering the system cold.

55.6%
faster on the redesigned interface — approve a single row of data
46%
faster on the redesigned interface — submit all approvals to complete the work
17
participants, none from Ligentia, testing generic non-supply-chain data

Alongside the efficiency gains, participants unfamiliar with the system were able to understand and operate the core interface elements without training, which is the clearest available evidence that the simplification in L5 is doing real work rather than being a stylistic preference.

This was self-initiated. The study was designed and run by the design team because the question needed answering, not because it was requested. The design team was planning a similar approach for milestones until that project was put on hold.

Next step

As we build closer ties with CX, look to test real-world applicability and monitor adoption post-launch. Share these findings to build awareness.

Composite personas: a new way of user testing

One piece of work worth flagging, given the difficulty of getting close to customers. Conventional practice is a handful of fixed personas, each a broad template of a customer type. We are building something more granular: a set of variables covering job roles, locations, the modules people use and the actions they commonly perform, which can be combined to represent many more customer situations than a small fixed set would.

The intent is to use AI analysis against those combinations to test design work across a far wider range of contexts than we could otherwise reach. It broadens coverage rather than replacing contact with real users, and it needs grounding in real customer data to be worth anything, which is another reason the research access ask matters.

This is early stage, with stakeholder conversations building out the detail. It is also unproven: we will not know whether the approach holds up in practice until we have tested it against real design work.

Next step

Complete the variable set and test the approach against live design work to establish whether it holds up.

Measuring the user's experience

Obtaining hard business-outcome metrics has been difficult at Ligentia. Where design has been able to measure directly, it has:

  • Lyssna: used to test prototype interaction patterns with external users and capture task-completion times, which gives a quantified measure of whether a design recommendation actually makes a task more efficient
  • Userflow: in-app onboarding and documentation, plus event tracking. Installed in Delivery, Wayfinder and Shipment Approval, the latter currently in staging
  • GA analytics: in use today for environmental data that informs design decisions: browser, screen resolution and device. This is how we confirmed an overwhelmingly desktop, Windows and Chrome user base, and a wide spread of screen resolutions with a strong bias toward 1920x1080, both of which directly constrain what we design for
  • Dovetail: research repository, intended to make research findings searchable and reusable rather than lost in documents. Loosely set up, and requires additional governance over how research is structured and tagged
  • Hotjar: screen recording with click and heat-map analysis. Installed in Delivery, but rarely used: it records all sessions indiscriminately, so internal testing activity contaminates the recordings. We are currently investigating IP filtering to exclude internal sessions, which would make the data usable. There is a strong research opportunity here once that is resolved
  • SUS surveys: the System Usability Scale produces a single standardised score, which makes perceived usability comparable over time and against other products rather than diagnosing specific problems. Design has run these previously, though not recently. A 2026 round is in the team goals, sequenced to follow the maturity survey

These are in active use and already inform design decisions. What is missing is not the tooling but the maturity of how we use it, which represents a strong opportunity for growth.

Self-directed platform and design system work

Some of design's time goes to platform vision work and design system improvement. These are not immediate product or CX requests. They get worked on when capacity allows. They are design-initiated, driven by me identifying space to articulate future value in usability and functionality, or to improve how the design system functions in terms of efficiency.

They are not prioritised by product leadership, but they have been consulted and agreement reached on the value.

Next step

Confirm you are happy with this working arrangement.

My rationale for them is that articulating a direction visually is far more effective than describing it verbally at Ligentia, and that this method is a proven mechanism for producing a forward view of the platform experience. It is unfunded and fits into gaps.

Why design may not be visible

The people who have worked closely with design recognise more than the output: the questions we ask, the assumptions we push back on, the alternative approaches explored and tested before one is chosen, the definition that gets tightened before anything is built. Outside those interactions, what is visible is a single screen, with no indication of the options that were considered and rejected, or why.

That is a visibility problem rather than a value problem. Within Product, visibility was reasonable, deliberately built through regular design crits with BA, Product and Engineering, the monthly Product team show-and-tells, and the stakeholder board described in section 3. The UX maturity survey benchmark above supports that: among respondents who work with design regularly, understanding of how design fits the process and of the reasoning behind its decisions both score at the top of the scale. Beyond that boundary it was more limited, and the reorganisation has moved design outside the group where visibility was high.

Next step

Extend this beyond Product to the wider business. Stakeholder support would make a material difference here.

03

How the work is managed day to day

Work management and intake

The team uses ClickUp as its work management system: a platform combining task tracking, documentation and reporting, where the same underlying tasks can be surfaced through different views depending on the audience.

The requirement it was chosen against was a single view of every active task across all modules, at whatever level of granularity is needed, from an individual task to the entire live picture. Design work moves across modules constantly, so a per-project view is not sufficient to manage it. We tested multiple tools against that requirement and settled on ClickUp. The decision was validated with product and engineering peers at the time.

We hold categories for all modules, including platform, and an intake request form for design requests, which allows us to triage incoming work efficiently rather than reactively.

ClickUp also acts as the team's centralised documentation repository.

The stakeholder board: cross-team visibility

On top of ClickUp we built a simplified stakeholder board: a lightweight view showing what is in progress across the design team, with a route to submit a request. It carries an active handoff view covering upcoming and completed work.

It exists because requests were arriving from multiple teams with conflicting priorities and no shared view of the whole, and because the full ClickUp view overloads casual viewers who only need to know current priority.

The board is the centrepiece of three short weekly priority meetings with key stakeholders across module and product work. Design work mixes short and long tasks with frequently moving priorities, so that visibility has been essential.

Internal review cadence

Alongside the stakeholder-facing meetings, the team runs its own weekly review of work undertaken, with a goals progress review every two weeks.

Each month the transcripts of those sessions are summarised using Claude and fed back to the team. That gives us a consolidated view of progress that would otherwise be spread across a series of separate conversations, and it is what the monthly goal scoring is based on.

Design crits

The team runs regular design crits with BA, Product and Engineering counterparts. These are where work in progress is reviewed cross-functionally before it is committed to: options tested against each other, assumptions challenged, and buildability checked with engineering while there is still time to change direction.

These are deliberately proportional rather than fixed. Who is involved varies with the complexity of the work. A straightforward change may only need the BA, while something touching multiple modules or with significant engineering implications pulls in a wider group.

They are also the main mechanism by which people outside design see how design reasons rather than only what it produces.

The cross-team process review

Earlier this year, changes in how teams were working, largely driven by AI entering everyday practice, broke parts of the existing process between product, BAs, design and engineering. Collaboration between teams stopped working smoothly, and significant friction was the result.

Design instigated and led the work to fix it, across four functions and without being asked to. We ran a retro to identify where the friction points actually were, then worked with each affected team on solutions rather than proposing a process at them. The result is a documented process flow that is clear to all contributors, and the working relationship is materially smoother than it was.

Relationship to DevOps

Design does not manage its work in DevOps but it does have a formal touchpoint in it: as part of the process review described above, design is now tagged on stories to confirm and sign off that the designs are approved before they progress.

ClickUp works because it gives stakeholders a single cross-module view; DevOps required tracking multiple boards across separate pages. If there is a case for consolidating onto one system across Tech, I am open to it. The requirement I would want to preserve is that single view, since it is what makes design's cross-module work visible and manageable.

Team and module ownership

Designers are assigned to their own modules wherever possible, so they build domain knowledge and relationships with the relevant stakeholders. They cross into other modules to support each other when required.

This is a loose indication of how designers are currently spread across work at a high level, not a fixed allocation. In practice it is considerably more fluid, and each designer leans into other projects as required.

It also shows me operating across most modules, which reflects my role as team lead and key reviewer of design work rather than a delivery load on each one.

How work is prioritised

Two things need separating. The product roadmap is what the business builds; I do not own it, and design supports and informs it. Design's own forward view is the team goals set out in section 2, which I lead.

Product roadmap prioritisation has typically run through the product team, most recently with Dennis and Laura, though both the approach and the ownership have changed several times.

Worth noting: the repeated changes in roadmap approach and ownership at product level have made forward planning difficult for design. Each change resets the working relationship and the basis for prioritisation. This sits outside design's control, so what I can do is hold design's own direction steady regardless, which is what the team goals provide. A stable product prioritisation route would let us plan further ahead, and matters more than which particular route it is.

Next step

Understand where product roadmap prioritisation will sit following the restructure.

How I kept senior stakeholders informed, and the current gap

Two mechanisms carried this previously:

  • A weekly 1:1 with Anthony Plummer, my senior stakeholder at the time. These ranged from updates on functionality in progress to monthly reporting on progress against the team goals, and sense-checking wider platform thinking with a senior voice.
  • A monthly Product team show-and-tell, which Dennis and I moved to a format of demonstrating work we had done together during the month. This was introduced specifically to address the visibility problem described in section 1. It gave a clear view of the business benefit the work contributed to, while exposing the thought process design and our BA counterparts had gone through: the problem-solving that is invisible when people only see a finished product. It was the most effective mechanism we had for making design's reasoning visible outside the immediate process, and the effect shows in our own tracking. Design visibility was the steadiest improving goal across the first half of the year, reaching full marks in June and July (section 2).

Both have now lapsed as a consequence of the restructure. The Anthony 1:1 no longer happens, and the future of the show-and-tells is uncertain.

This bears on your question about design's value: with the team changes, there is a risk that what was working before is simply lost.

I would like to pick up something equivalent: a regular session where design demonstrates work in progress and the reasoning behind it, to whichever audience makes most sense now. It is a straightforward thing to restart, and probably the cheapest available step on the visibility side.

Next step

Discuss the format and audience, and how this might work.

04

Existing platform work versus new

You said you were unclear on the split between existing Ligentix work and new. From design's side:

L4 is not a meaningful category of design work. We do not undertake design work on L4. There is a widely held understanding that it is being sunset, so design support has been minimised to occasional consultation where something specific requires it. Design effort is directed at everything else.

L5 work is driven by product requests, typically arriving via Dennis and the BAs. Distribution across modules is not consistent and varies week to week, which is why the stakeholder board and the weekly priority meetings described in section 3 exist. The work moves faster than a fixed allocation could track.

When that work is quieter, the team advances its own goals, as set out in section 2.

Ligentix One

As I understand it, you are working on Ligentix One, and my understanding is that it is a ground-up rebuild. I would welcome correction and additional detail.

You have suggested I may become involved in Ligentix One. This raises an important question: if the business goal is moving off L5, it would follow that design resource should begin to shift to support it. At present all of design's effort is directed at L5.

Next step

Understand the longer term intent, and what it means for design's resourcing.

Design's role as Ligentix One progresses

Ligentix One is in stealth, and there is good reason for that. Every additional contributor adds opinions and slows things down. I am not proposing widening that group now.

What I would ask is that when it does widen, design is a core part of that group rather than brought in to style the result. The value at that point is advocating for usability as decisions are being made, and being positioned to run legitimate usability testing as the work becomes testable. I would be ready to join at whatever point you judge appropriate.

On testing specifically, customer access is the harder problem. Internal review has to come first, and CX will reasonably not want customers seeing something before they have. But customer testing is not the only route. Interaction patterns can be validated with external participants who have no connection to Ligentia, which is how we have tested prototypes previously via Lyssna. That tells us whether a pattern is learnable and efficient, without exposing anything commercially sensitive or going near a customer.

Next step

Agree the mechanism for design to join this group as it widens.

Claude Code and Claude Design

Claude Design was disabled following a request from Karolina on cost grounds. We were using it minimally at the time (testing capabilities and how it could fit into our working processes), so agreeing to it was pragmatic rather than a loss. If it becomes available again we would be glad to continue.

Our working methods are changing with the times. Recent design iterations have started in Claude Code for myself and Chuka, while Adrian was assessing Claude Design. Both routes are about exploring ideas and variations at a high level without worrying about visual refinement. That workflow has proven very productive for getting through multiple concepts quickly. Refinement then moves to Figma Design, and there is still a back and forth between the two that neither tool closes cleanly, although it is improving quickly. Claude Design and Figma Make are both aimed at bridging that gap, with the end point being a fully interactive prototype that could go straight into usability testing without queuing behind engineering.

Token costs remain high for Claude Design and Figma Make, which is the honest counterweight to that, and gives me pause on these tools as long term solutions (designers like to make LOTS of changes). We remain open minded about their potential adoption. This space is moving so quickly that tools, practices and workarounds are changing almost by the day. The team stays fully engaged with the conversation around these tools and discusses them regularly.

Ideally the team would keep access to Claude Design while this settles, though I would want that on a different footing than before. We have had no visibility into token expenditure or whether any usage limits exist, which makes the cost impossible to manage from our side. Whether it becomes a long term solution or simply remains a long term option is not something I can answer yet.

Next step

Establish what guardrails are available around token spend, so we can work within them and continue testing as the tool matures.

Flagged for the goals review

  • Paid Lyssna
  • Hotjar expansion, once the data contamination issue is resolved
  • A defined cross-functional group across design, engineering and product, with the authority to place research-driven work onto the product roadmap
06

Design as a consultancy function

Some people in the global team are building their own tools using AI coding tools. There is genuine opportunity in that enthusiasm and it is going to keep happening, so the question is not whether to allow it but, in my opinion, what needs to be in place around it.

What it does change is the shape of design's role. I expect that over time design teams in businesses like ours will be as much consultants as executors, because the volume of things being made will exceed what any small team could produce itself. That is a reasonable direction and I would rather design adapt to it deliberately than be bypassed by it.

The practical implication is about expectations and guardrails, and design is only one part of that. The risks with tools built this way go well beyond usability and visual consistency, with security being the more serious one, and that sits outside design's competence entirely. Whatever is put in place needs the relevant expertise, not just mine.

Where design does have a legitimate part to play is anything heading toward customers. It is worth someone having looked at it from a brand and product experience perspective before it goes, and design is well placed to be that consultation. Ligentia's customers are worldwide, and inconsistency in what reaches them is a harder problem to unpick later than to prevent now.

I am not proposing a specific mechanism here, since you will have a clearer view than I do of what would work across the wider organisation.

Next step

Include design in the conversation about what guardrails are put in place.

07

People

No headcount request. Current resource is appropriate to the work in front of us.

The caveat: with teams being reorganised and expectations of the newly split teams not yet clear, that could change. I am not expecting it to currently, and I will flag it early if it does.

What design will commit to

For now the team continues as established: delivering against the team goals, and working with the BAs on module work as it comes through. That continuity matters through a restructure.

Beyond that, some of the next quarter depends on decisions that are not mine. With the reorganisation there will be a period of working out how the new teams operate together, what new ways of working are needed, and what additional design work follows from that. I would rather say that plainly than commit to a plan built on assumptions.

What I will commit to is the research access work. Recent conversations have been positive, and getting designers directly in front of customers is the single change that would most improve what design can evidence. I expect to make real progress on that this quarter and will report on it.
